item.title: Astra can read and write weights to improve Qwen
item.abstract:
We find that frontier LLMs are surprisingly good at natively reading and writing neural network weights , using a variety of recent tools and algorithms or even via direct weight editing. These results show sparks of Weight-Space Programming, which may extend beyond what we’d expect from humans or conventional algorithms. This might be a big deal for both optimization and interpretability. Just by looking at the raw weights, GPT-6 Astra can tell what a network was trained to do . And without any environment feedback, it has no trouble writing, from scratch, small game-playing networks that outplay networks trained with PPO for 100 million steps. Likewise, asked to make Qwen3.5-0.8B better at math without gradients, Astra identifies an issue in its weights causing reasoning loops that Qwen’s own model card warns about, and fixes this by natively editing 0.016% of the weights . With the same sampling settings, this weight correction raises MATH-500 from 7.9% to 48.1% and generalizes out of the box to instruction following, raising IFEval by 3x. All of this is possible without allowing Astra to write training loops. It uses its reasoning to figure out what each part of a neural network computes, or should compute, and changes the weights accordingly. We call this Weight-Space Programming . Throughout the history of deep learning, we encoded our simplistic inductive biases into tiny symbolic optimizers like Adam or Muon. This is changing: our neural network weights will soon be natively optimized by LLMs that deliberately reason about their weights . If you were asked to handcraft a neural network that plays Go, what would you do? If you were handed raw neural network weights and asked to predict their behavior, where would you even start? For almost any human, this is practically impossible. Today, weights are written by optimization , by custom networks trained to write them , or by compilers from formal programs . In this post, we find that the current generation of frontier LLMs, used natively in natural language, are starting to become eerily good at understanding and crafting neural network weights around natural-language goals. For a few years now, we’ve all been using LLMs to optimize text artifacts like prompts and the programs built around them . More recently, we’ve started using them to optimize whole harnesses and the training code and hyperparameters that train ML models . We often justified these methods by reference to the fact that we don’t know other principled ways to hill-climb on text artifacts, unlike for updating the weights of differentiable neural networks . After all, humans can “optimize” code by hand, for example, so it made sense to ask LLMs to do it, but they can’t “optimize” neural weights by hand, so those remained largely in the realm of symbolic algorithms. In this post, we share very early results that allow us to argue that the paradigm of reasoning-driven optimization is now coming even for differentiable neural networks . In Weight-Space Programming , a general-purpose LLM reads and writes a network’s weights directly (i.e., not through an optimizer, and in particular not with gradient descent) around some natural language spec, sometimes even with no environment feedback at all. In natural language, it’s becoming possible to “just ask” an LLM to natively find a hidden trait or failure inside the weights of a neural network, to fix that failure, or to write a new network from scratch . We report early, exciting results on each of these below, first on small networks and then even on real language models: We start with a small-scale experiment to see if LLMs can understand the continuous weight space, which is essentially just a list of numbers. In our first experiments, we train some neural network with some algorithm. It would be extremely exciting if the LLM is able to tell its behavior just from the weights. We trained neural network policies with PPO to play four computer games. All four networks take the same input channels, choose from the same actions, and have exactly the same network dimensions, so that it is not able to tell unless the weights are read. For each of these networks, we pass its raw weights into Astra as a prompt, and ask: Which game was this neural network trained on? Without revealing the options of the games we consider, Astra was still able to name the right game for all four networks. This is exciting particularly because there are so many games out there that Astra could choose from. It seems that Astra was able to work out what game each network was built to play, just from features of its weights. For example, where each input channel’s first-layer weights concentrate (e.g., for Breakout, the agent’s weights lie along the bottom row, a paddle), and which actions the output layer tells apart. Next, we wanted to see if this generalizes to other tasks and models. We train diffusion models (DDPM) to generate circle, triangle, and square images independently. We then ask Astra if it could tell what the DDPMs are trained to generate, just from the weights alone. We do not allow tool use or forward passes. Astra was able to tell what each model generates, from the weights alone. It finds the shape in the output layer, where each hidden unit’s weights draw one piece of the shape’s edge, and it draws just those edges. Interestingly, it draws every shape as an outline, ignoring that the actual models generate filled shapes. This mistake kind of shows it does not rely on calculating the forward pass, but rather it actually reads the structure/geometry of the weights. Now, in the first two experiments above, Astra was not really looking at the full network and could get away with only reading the first or the last layers. This is not a scalable strategy for larger (particularly language) models and problems we really care about, as how they process and think through their input often happens in the intermediate layers. So next, we take the first and last layers away and leave Astra with only the middle layers. We train three small language models (7.2M parameters) to predict the next character, one each on Python code The Python code dataset, as a list of its files with a script that rebuilds it: GitHub . , Japanese in alphabet (romaji) , and English . We then remove the input and output layers and give Astra only the four transformer blocks in between. Without these two layers, nothing in the weights says which character is which, and the model cannot be run on any text. Astra may analyze the weights with Python, but it may not run the network or any of its layers on any input. We ask: which language was this network trained on, and what each of its 24 attention heads does . Astra names the right language for all three networks, in both of its attempts. It also finds every copying head (induction head), the heads that let a model repeat text it has seen earlier, and names no other head as one. The reasoning went like this. To tell Python apart, Astra looked for copying heads, which let a model repeat earlier text, such as completing tot to tot al when tot al came before. Without running anything, it found a first-layer head that looks one character back and then, by multiplying weight matrices, the later heads that search using what that head brings along ( Figure 1 ). We find that this is actually a method presented by Elhage et al. , which we never mentioned to Astra. Code repeats names far more than prose, so many copying heads pointed to Python. Romaji stood out instead because the last of the four blocks it was given (not the output layer, which was removed) writes in fewer distinct directions, as if the model had fewer letters to tell apart. Indeed, romaji never uses some letters like q, l, v and x. So far, Astra has only read weights. Now, we ask if Astra knows how to write the weights. We train a PPO network to operate a car such that it can scale a ramp in a Kinetix environment .

item.title: Progress on provable inference for large language models
item.abstract: Chapter 01 : Executive summary Roy Rinberg (Anthropic), Alex Allain (Anthropic); Alessandro Chiesa (EPFL, StarkWare), Miranda Christ (MIT, RESI), Rahul Dalal (Anthropic STEM Fellows Program, Succinct), Giacomo Fenzi (EPFL), Ben Mayer (Anthropic Fellows Program, MIT), Guy Weissenberg (EPFL) Executive summary When you talk to a friend in person, you have many ways to know it is really them: you can see them, hear them, shake their hand. When you talk to an AI model, you have almost none. A user querying a model today cannot check that the responses came from the specific model that a developer claims is responding, as opposed to one secretly substituted in by a routing service for cost reasons, or even by an attacker who has tampered with the token stream. Judging from the model’s output alone is unreliable, even if it produces high-quality responses. Cryptographic proofs of inference solve this problem: they let a model provider commit to a model and then prove that each response was produced by that model. Such proofs could enable applications ranging from consumer products to internal security, and could contribute to a toolkit for verifying compliance with AI pacing requirements. Specifically, we have made progress on a powerful type of cryptographic proof known as a “zkSNARK”, which is uniquely fit for provable inference (owing to its strong hiding and efficiency properties). In this post, we share some of that progress, primarily through a system we call FlashProve. A brief technical summary is as follows: Claude has produced improvements on zkSNARKs for inference, building a system that is substantially faster than prior open-source systems. For a large model (Llama 4 Maverick, 400B-parameter mixture of experts), a single H100 GPU generates proofs at around 110 tokens/second, with a proof size of ~19 MB per 1,024-token request, when in 4-bit quantized weights, using integer arithmetic in prefill. This is ~70-95x the GPU time of running the model itself on vLLM, a common open-source library. Prior open-source systems are orders of magnitude slower, as we discuss in section 6 . Claude found novel ways to apply state-of-the-art tools in the cryptography and security literature, while relying on well-established design principles for cryptographic proof systems. The commitment to the model, and subsequent inference proofs, hide the weights of the model; hiding the architecture of the model is not a goal of this system. Claude is good at optimization, but often makes decisions that are hard to evaluate, especially in large complex systems. We counter this by providing top-level auditable statements in Lean (a formal verification language) for the claimed security guarantees. Today we are releasing five artifacts: The current blog post, which outlines our system and its potential applications; A technical report explaining the details of our system; A (Claude-written) protocol specification document; Executable code that includes: a prover and two verifiers, a fast verifier in C++, and a provably correct verifier in Lean; and Lean proofs for the top level mathematical statements, along with an interactive visualizer of the Lean theorems to aid with auditing. We release our code, Lean proofs, and documentation under the Apache 2.0 license. 1 This research post is meant to share intermediate progress, and not a completed research agenda. We are sharing this explicitly with the goal that others look at what we have done, take it, and improve it. Introduction When a user sends a request to an AI model, today they have no way of knowing for certain that the model they selected is the one that generated the response. For everyday uses, in which users mostly care about the output and not necessarily which specific model produced it, this is a less pressing concern. But there are several cases where such assurance would be useful. For example, independent evaluators who test AI models before and after release need to know that the model they are evaluating is the model being served. Clients who use a model through a third-party routing service want assurance that the tokens came from the model they paid for. And if a cyberattacker modifies the token stream while pretending to be a given model, a user has no way to detect it from the output alone. However, enabling verification of model responses is challenging. Most frontier models’ weights are kept private, and even if the user had access to the weights, checking that a given response was produced by a model with those weights would involve running the model, which requires computational resources far beyond what a typical user (or even evaluator) can afford. The goal of provable inference (PI) is to enable a user with limited computational resources and without any information about the weights to verify that a response came from the requested model. PI is motivated both by a desire to increase customer trust in AI providers, and—because it can be used to provide assurances to independent evaluators and allows providers to demonstrate that they are meeting certain commitments and legal obligations—it also has implications for pacing the frontier of AI development and for AI regulation. One way to implement PI is via a cryptographic object called a zero-knowledge succinct argument: the model provider sends, along with the claimed response, a short proof (say, a few megabytes) that the user can quickly verify (ideally, in seconds on a CPU). If the claimed response deviates from the specified model, the user’s check will fail. Importantly, cryptographic techniques ensure that the proof reveals nothing about the model’s weights. Today, we release FlashProve: an open-source performant prototype for provable inference . For a 400B-parameter mixture-of-experts model (Llama 4 Maverick, 4-bit quantization), we show that a single H100 GPU generates proofs at over 100 tokens/second, with proof size of ~19 MB per 1,024-token request (~70-95 times the GPU time that vLLM, a common open-source library, takes to process prompts of the same length). The release comes with executable code, Lean formalization, and a technical description of the protocol. Our aim is twofold: (i) accelerating and facilitating the development of provable inference; and (ii) demonstrating that zero-knowledge succinct arguments are practical for provable inference. We believe that this progress has meaningful implications for security, in pacing AI development , in providing AI customers with integrity guarantees , in facilitating tooling for auditors and regulators , and more. Trust challenges in AI proliferation The development of artificial intelligence and its growing role in our digital infrastructure and economy raises trust challenges that AI providers must answer. Addressing these and other challenges is facilitated by relying on tools for provable inference (PI). Tools for PI include hardware approaches, software approaches, or a combination of both. Here, we focus on a software-only approach: a cryptographic tool known as a “zkSNARK” ( zero-knowledge succinct argument of knowledge ). Informally, a zkSNARK is a system allowing a prover to convince a verifier , by way of a short “certificate”, that a given computation was executed correctly; crucially, the certificate is zero-knowledge in that it reveals no information beyond what is implied by the computation’s correctness and is succinct in that it’s exponentially faster to verify compared to the proved computation. Below we outline several challenges and how zkSNARKs help in addressing them. Challenge 1: pacing Some proposals to regulate and pace AI development rely on monitoring hardware and how it is used . For example, a provider might be required to devote its hardware to inference rather than to training a powerful new model. The provider might try to cheat by serving cheaper models or using compute in an unexpected way, freeing up resources for training.

item.title: Zyphra AI Introduces Zyphra Hierarchical Attention (ZHA): A Path to True Subquadratic Attention
item.abstract: Zyphra has released Zyphra Hierarchical Attention (ZHA) , a sparse attention method built around a tree-structured indexer. ZHA targets a known gap in sparse attention: the indexer that picks tokens still scans the whole context. Zyphra’s technical paper shows ZHA can be distilled into frozen pretrained models with about 4B tokens. On Qwen3.6-35B-A3B it stays close to dense attention on reasoning, agentic coding and 256K retrieval benchmarks. ZHA is a sparse attention method from Zyphra that finds relevant keys by searching a tree. It keeps the full KV cache. The tree only decides which cached keys each query reads. Fixed-state methods like SSMs and sliding windows saturate at long contexts. Fine-grained sparse methods like DeepSeek Sparse Attention score every past token with an indexer. The final attention is sparse, but the indexer still grows with the full context. Near 1M tokens, cited work shows indexing takes 60 to 90% of layer time. ZHA makes the search itself sparse. ZHA splits keys into contiguous chunks and compresses each chunk into a summary key. Summaries are grouped and compressed again, level by level. With chunk size 4, 6 levels cover 4,096 tokens per top node. Summaries come from a small set of learned reference queries . Each reference query gives a tangent-plane estimate of a chunk’s log attention mass. The max over these planes approximates how much attention any future query would give the chunk. At decode time, a query scores the top-level nodes. It keeps the smallest set holding a fraction p of estimated attention mass. It then expands only those children, repeating until it reaches raw KV entries. Top-p makes the budget adaptive. A single-fact lookup touches few branches. A query that needs many scattered facts expands more. The first token is always kept as an attention sink. Zyphra team converted Qwen3.6-35B-A3B with 2 trees: deep (chunk 4, 6 levels) and wide (chunk 256, 1 level). Both use 16 reference queries and p = 0.95. It also trained a MiniMax Sparse Attention (MSA) indexer on 40B tokens, 10x ZHA’s budget. Source: arXiv 2610.42112 , Figure 5. All numbers self-reported by Zyphra. The biggest gap is on retrieval. MSA drops to 77.1% on RULER-13, while both ZHA trees stay above 93%. On LongBench v2, the deep tree and MSA read similar key shares (1.1% vs 1%). The deep tree scores 14.1 points higher. Across 28 tree geometries, RULER accuracy held steady when attending to 10 to 30% of keys. At fixed compression, deeper trees kept accuracy at higher sparsity. A 4-parameter model predicts RULER accuracy from geometry with 1.44-point RMSE. Zyphra released no kernels. It modeled decode latency for one layer at batch size 1 with a roofline. The lightweight setting uses 1 reference query, chunk 8 and p = 0.75. In that model, ZHA beats dense attention near 48K tokens and MSA near 0.48M tokens. At 1B tokens, projected speedups reach 373 to 417x over dense and 52 to 58x over MSA. The blog post adds 32 to 35x and 4.7 to 5.1x at 10M tokens. At 256K, the modeled gains are modest. Pareto-frontier settings reach 1.93x to 2.28x over dense, at 92.7 to 96.4% RULER-13. Routing and selection add their own cost. The base model stays frozen. Only the reference queries train. A KL loss matches dense attention mass per chunk at every level. Qwen and Nemotron runs used 3.98B tokens over 1,900 steps at 32K context. Zyphra reports models under 1B parameters struggled during conversion. Results improved sharply at 4B and above. Check out the ZHA paper on arXiv and Zyphra’s technical blog . item.title: Qwen 3.8 27B on my laptop can interpret model weights, too
item.abstract: Yesterday’s hot paper was Sparks of Weight-Space Programming: LLMs can natively read & write neural network weights by Rikiya Takehi, Jayden Teoh, Alex Zhang, and Omar Khattab. The paper (OK, the authors classify is as a “blog post”, but it’s paper-shaped) found that frontier models, in particular GPT-6 Astra, can both interpret and modify the raw weights of a machine learning model—literally a text description of the model containing a bunch of floating point numbers. I’ve been playing with one of the examples from the paper and I’m delighted to share that Qwen 3.8 27B running on my laptop can do this as well! Here’s the highlight from their abstract, describing impressive capabilities for GPT-6 Astra and coining the term Weight-Space Programming for when LLMs analyze and modify model weights: Just by looking at the raw weights, GPT-6 Astra can tell what a network was trained to do . And without any environment feedback, it has no trouble writing, from scratch, small game-playing networks that outplay networks trained with PPO for 100 million steps. Likewise, asked to make Qwen3.5-0.8B better at math without gradients, Astra identifies an issue in its weights causing reasoning loops that Qwen’s own model card warns about, and fixes this by natively editing 0.016% of the weights . With the same sampling settings, this weight correction raises MATH-500 from 7.9% to 48.1% and generalizes out of the box to instruction following, raising IFEval by 3x. All of this is possible without allowing Astra to write training loops. It uses its reasoning to figure out what each part of a neural network computes, or should compute, and changes the weights accordingly. We call this Weight-Space Programming . The paper combines two topics that I think deserve to be treated separately. The first is what models can do with raw weights without running tools or executing code. The second explores how well models, once armed with code, can run operations to update and improve other models. spaCy author Matthew Honnibal called the paper misleading for conflating the two, and Sean Goedecke deconstructed the Qwen3.5-0.8B update example as taking the same steps that a human ML researcher would use. I’m going to focus on the no-tools question, which I think is the more interesting of the two. The paper presents the first question as Can LLMs understand model behaviors from weights? They trained four neural networks to play simplified 10x10 grid versions of four classic computer games—Breakout, Pong, Pac-Man, and Freeway (I had to look that one up , it’s an Atari 2600 game from 1981). Then they fed those weights (as floating point numbers) to an LLM along with the following question: The weights below belong to one policy network that was trained with reinforcement learning to play a game on this grid. Which game was it trained on? Work from the weights. You have no tools: no code execution, no calculator, nothing to run. This is a single response. The GitHub repository that accompanies the paper is RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs . The exp1_which_game folder contains the prompts they used, with weights for the four games: I checked and, aside from the weights, each prompt is identical to the others. The prompts on GitHub are self-contained. My LLM tool has a -f/--fragment option which can be passed the URL to a text file to use as a prompt, which means I can run any of the above like this: This example requires the llm-openrouter plugin installed, and runs the Breakout prompt against Kimi K3.1 Pro via OpenRouter. Here’s what I got back from Kimi K3.1 Pro , which successfully guessed Breakout after 9m 41s and 19,493 reasoning tokens. But how about Qwen 3.8 27B ? That’s still my favorite model to run on my own laptop—it’s just 17GB (I use this version ) and somehow feels close to the leading proprietary models of 2025. I fired up LM Studio , ensured Qwen 3.8 27B was loaded with a long context window (the default 8192 context failed with errors), installed the llm-lmstudio plugin and ran this command: (I had to bump the timeout up using an environment variable, see this issue .) After 46m 12s and 43,506 reasoning tokens, Qwen on my laptop returned a response that ended like this (here’s the reasoning trace ): Game: A simplified Pac-Man-style gridworld: an agent moves through a fixed 8x8 maze with central and corner wall blocks, moving objects/ghosts, and reward targets/pellets. Description: The agent navigates a fixed maze-like 8x8 board, using current agent/moving-object/previous-frame cues to move through corridors, collect reward-target cells, and avoid moving objects or hazards. This is impressive. I tried it on two of the other games as well. It identified Pong ( reasoning ) in 1h 4m 54s: Pong — specifically a Pong-like paddle/ball game where the agent controls a vertical paddle on the right side and must move up/down to intercept or return a moving ball/reward object. The agent moves a right-side paddle vertically to hit or catch a moving ball-like reward target moving across the 8×8 field, while a left-side moving object/opponent and wall borders define the play; reward is obtained by successfully intercepting/returning/scoring the ball, and missing or failing to hit it is penalized. And Breakout ( reasoning ) in 52m 25s: Game: Breakout, or an Arkanoid-like paddle/ball/brick game. Description: The agent is a paddle on the bottom row and moves left/right to keep a ball in play; the ball moves around the upper grid, and bricks/reward targets in the top rows give reward when hit, while missing the ball/hitting the bottom wall ends the episode or gives penalty. Qwen failed at the Freeway prompt, which didn’t surprise me considering that game is more obscure than the other three. Here’s that transcript —Qwen thought it was “A simplified Pac-Man-like grid game: agent moves 4-directionally”. The reasoning traces are fun to skim, and almost incomprehensible. Here’s a sample: What about agent channel0? We see some large channel0 rows near row8 col7/8 and maybe bottom? Let’s list channel0 large: line436 input435 (row8 col7 ch0) -2.107,1.169,0.513...; line441 input440 (row8 col8 ch0) -0.376,0.010,1.564,3.855...; line445 input444 (row8 col8 ch4) 0.142,0.491...; line382? input381 ch0? Wait line382 input381: 381//5=76 (row7 col6), ch1? 381%5=1? 76 * 5=380, ch1. So not. Channel0 large maybe at row8 col7/8 only. Also top row? line44 input43 ch3, line49 ch3. Channel0 large maybe not many. Agent position could be near bottom-right? If the agent is typically at bottom-right? That said though, I expect a sufficiently experienced human being armed with a notepad and a pencil could get there with enough effort. It’s a cool paper, but some of the wider commentary I’ve seen around it does not feel justified. I’m not ready to declare that the age of source code is over and our future involves incomprehensible machines editing their own model weights in incomprehensible ways. item.title: NVIDIA Shows 3 Ways to Speed Up MoE Inference on DGX Spark, Lifting Ling-3.0-flash Throughput 42.5%
item.abstract: NVIDIA’s latest technical blog shows how to speed up mixture-of-experts (MoE) inference on one DGX Spark . The test model is Ant Group inclusionAI’s Ling-3.0-flash , a 124B-parameter MoE with 5.1B active parameters. NVIDIA stacked three optimizations: a new MoE kernel backend, an FP8 output layer and built-in speculative decoding. On all 1,319 GSM8K questions, decode throughput rose 42.5% with no statistically detectable accuracy change. So why is it relevant for Devs? DGX Spark is a desktop system, not a data center node. NVIDIA’s results show a 124B MoE serving single-user requests faster on that desk-side box. The technical post also shows where MoE decode time goes, and how to cut it. DGX Spark is NVIDIA’s desktop system built on the GB10 Grace Blackwell Superchip. It offers 128 GB of unified memory and 273 GB/s of memory bandwidth. Peak compute is up to 1 petaFLOP of sparse FP4. NVIDIA rates it for inference on models up to 200B parameters. In the NVIDIA technical post , the NVIDIA team profiled Ling-3.0-flash-fp4 at batch size 1. Decoding was memory-bound: reading model weights drove execution time. Two operations stood out, the MoE computation and the LM head that scores the vocabulary. That points to two levers: move fewer bytes per decode step, and generate more tokens per verification round. The baseline followed the official W4A8 recipe. It used FlashInfer MXFP4 MoE kernels, CUTLASS dense GEMM and an FP32 LM-head path. On a synthetic 32K-input, 2K-output test, it ran at 27.71 ms per token (36.09 tokens per second). 1. Humming MXFP4 MoE kernels: NVIDIA swapped FlashInfer’s MoE backend for Humming , an independent kernel library. Humming uses NVRTC to compile kernels at runtime for the actual matrix shapes, data types and GPU. That includes the narrow 768-wide expert layer. Each kernel compiles in seconds. The FlashInfer CUTLASS path compiles 97 targets with ninja, on the order of tens of minutes. Throughput rose 9.3% to 39.45 tokens per second. 2. Online FP8 LM head: The LM head is a 157,184 x 2,560 matrix stored in BF16. Every generated token reads all of it. Quantizing only this layer to FP8 at load time halves those reads. Setting SGLANG_ENABLE_FP8_LM_HEAD=1 enables it. It cannot be combined with the baseline –enable-fp32-lm-head option. Combined with Humming, throughput reached 43.94 tokens per second. That is 21.7% over baseline and 11.4% over Humming alone. 3. MTP speculative decoding with NEXTN: Ling-3.0-flash ships with a built-in NEXTN prediction layer, so no extra draft model is needed. It drafts three tokens, and the model verifies four positions at once. Verification costs about 2.26x a normal decode step. The main cost is MoE, not attention. Verifying four tokens can activate up to 32 experts instead of 8. On the synthetic test, an average of 3.90 tokens were accepted per round. Throughput jumped to 102.88 tokens per second, up 185.1%. The three techniques do not overlap. Humming and the FP8 LM head cut the cost of each step. MTP cuts the number of steps. The integration trap: Stacking these is not automatic. With FP8 LM head and MTP both on, the draft must share the full LM-head module. Otherwise the framework silently falls back, and the draft interprets FP8 weights as BF16. Accept length drops to 1.00, and throughput falls below the unoptimized baseline. The NVIDIA team advises checking at startup that each optimization is active. NVIDIA points to the Ling cookbook notebook for enabling both together. Synthetic tests flatter speculative decoding, so the NVIDIA team also ran all 1,319 GSM8K questions. It used 5-shot prompting with chain-of-thought, temperature 0.6, top_p 0.95 and top_k 29. With all three optimizations, time per output token fell from 26.45 ms to 18.56 ms. Decode throughput rose 42.5%, from 37.81 to 53.89 tokens per second. Mean latency dropped 24.5%, from 15.21 to 11.49 seconds. Accuracy moved from 96.89% to 96.82%, a change NVIDIA calls statistically undetectable. Accept length here was 2.68, versus 3.90 on synthetic data. The NVIDIA team gives three reasons for the gap. Synthetic outputs are more repetitive, so drafts are accepted more often. The synthetic test used greedy decoding, while GSM8K used sampling. GSM8K answers are also short, with a median near 310 tokens versus a fixed 2K. Ling-3.0-flash belongs to Ant Group inclusionAI’s Ling 3.0 family , released under the MIT license. The open-weight lineup also includes Ling-3.0-tiny , a 7.9B MoE with 1.3B active parameters. Both come with base checkpoints and FP8, INT4 and GGUF builds; flash also has FP4. OpenRouter also lists inclusionAI’s vision-language, finance and health variants built on Ling 3.0 Flash. Ling-3.0-flash is built to keep per-token cost low: On its model card , inclusionAI reports 56.6 on SWE-Bench Pro and 72.4 on SWE-Bench Multilingual. It also reports 93.2 on MathArena AIME 2026 and 87.0 on HMMT Feb 2026. Artificial Analysis results shown on OpenRouter list 85.5% on GPQA Diamond and 55.4% on Terminal-Bench 2.1. The hardest reasoning tests remain tough: Humanity’s Last Exam scores 22.7 self-reported and 23.7% independently. API pricing: Artificial Analysis lists InclusionAI’s API at $0.075 per 1M input tokens and $0.22 per 1M output tokens. That blends to about $0.05 per 1M tokens, using its 7:2:1 cache-hit, input and output mix. It measured output speed at 231.7 tokens per second, third of 26 models in its class. On OpenRouter , Novita and DeepInfra list $0.06 input and $0.18 output. Against peers: Artificial Analysis lists higher blended prices for comparable models. Step 3.7 Flash is $0.18, Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite $0.33 and GPT-5 (medium) $1.34. These figures compare price only; they are not quality-adjusted. Quantization costs little quality: inclusionAI’s quantization table compares BF16, FP8, INT4 and FP4. FP4 scores 83.68 on GPQA-diamond versus 84.97 in BF16. IFBench moves from 74.49 to 73.87, and ArcPrize from 68.75 to 68.06. SciCode shows the largest drop, from 41.24 to 38.43. The FP4 checkpoint is the one NVIDIA ran on DGX Spark. NVIDIA’s full analysis is on the NVIDIA Technical Blog . Model weights and recipes are on Hugging Face , the SGLang cookbook and the Ling cookbook . The post NVIDIA Shows 3 Ways to Speed Up MoE Inference on DGX Spark, Lifting Ling-3.0-flash Throughput 42.5% appeared first on MarkTechPost .

item.title: Building ultra-low-latency voice AI applications on AWS
item.abstract: Conversational AI is transforming how humans interact with technology. From virtual assistants and AI-powered contact centers to real-time translation and accessibility tools, voice-first interfaces are rapidly becoming the default mode of interaction for millions of users worldwide. Yet delivering a truly natural voice experience remains one of the hardest challenges in AI infrastructure. Users expect human-like responsiveness. Excess latency can break conversational flow and erode trust. To feel natural, AI-generated speech must arrive within the same temporal window as human turn-taking. This post introduces how Cartesia , an AWS Partner specializing in real-time voice AI, uses purpose-built State Space Models (SSMs) and AWS infrastructure to deliver sub-100ms text-to-speech and speech-to-text at global scale. Developers can build voice experiences that feel indistinguishable from human conversation. The demand for real-time voice AI is growing rapidly across industries: Traditional transformer-based text-to-speech (TTS) models struggle with streaming latency because they process entire sequences before producing output. This architectural limitation creates a fundamental tension: higher quality often means higher latency. A new class of models, State Space Models, resolves this trade-off. State Space Models (SSMs) take a fundamentally different approach to processing sequences than transformers, the architecture behind most of today’s AI. Transformers use a mechanism called attention, which compares every element in a sequence to every other element. As a result, the amount of computation grows quadratically as the sequence gets longer. SSMs instead treat a sequence as a system that evolves continuously over time, processing it step by step and carrying a compact internal state forward. This can be converted into a form computers handle efficiently, keeping the cost low for certain long sequences. This efficiency makes SSMs well suited to real-time, streaming data like live speech. Key advantages of SSMs for audio processing include: These properties make SSMs uniquely suited for real-time voice applications where both quality and latency are non-negotiable. Cartesia puts these SSM advantages to work in two production voice models: Sonic for speech generation and Ink for transcription. Cartesia is a real-time multimodal intelligence company that has built a voice AI application, purpose-built on State Space Model architecture. Founded by researchers who pioneered SSM advances, Cartesia’s application is designed for streaming inference at the edge of human perception. The application features two core models, Sonic for text-to-speech and Ink for speech-to-text, both optimized for sub-100ms first-byte latency while maintaining studio-quality output. Sonic is Cartesia’s flagship streaming text-to-speech model, delivering ultra-realistic speech synthesis with sub-100ms latency: Sonic is recommended for teams that want the fastest time-to-production with minimal operational overhead. Call the API and receive streaming audio in real time. Ink is Cartesia’s streaming speech-to-text model, purpose-built for conversational AI applications: Together, Sonic and Ink provide the complete voice AI stack needed to build conversational agents that feel human. If you need data sovereignty, latency control, or compliance, you can deploy Cartesia models directly into your own AWS account. Sonic is delivered as an Amazon SageMaker AI model package through AWS Marketplace, which you deploy to a SageMaker AI endpoint running entirely within your virtual private cloud (VPC). Inference data doesn’t leave your account. The deployment patterns in this section cover Sonic. Ink is currently available through the Cartesia API, which you can purchase through the Cartesia Voice AI Platform listing in AWS Marketplace. Two primary patterns are available for Sonic. Deploying on Amazon SageMaker AI is the fastest path to a managed, in-VPC Sonic endpoint. Sonic ships as an AWS Marketplace model package, so there’s a one-time subscribe step that grants your account an AWS Region-specific model-package ARN. You then create the SageMaker AI endpoint from that ARN, either from the console or with the SageMaker or Boto3 SDK. The following steps follow Cartesia’s official deployment notebook. Run from an Amazon SageMaker Notebook Instance or SageMaker Studio. The AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) execution role needs AmazonSageMakerFullAccess . To subscribe, your role (and you) need aws-marketplace:Subscribe , aws-marketplace:Unsubscribe , and aws-marketplace:ViewSubscriptions . Otherwise, the account must already be subscribed to the listing. Before deployment, choose a supported instance type from the model package’s SupportedRealtimeInferenceInstanceTypes field: If your chosen instance type’s applied value is below your current usage plus your planned endpoint instance count, you may need to request a service quota increase. See SageMaker AI quotas for details. In Amazon SageMaker JumpStart, you can subscribe to its AWS Marketplace model package, create a SageMaker model, and host it on a real-time endpoint. The following four steps show the deployment path. Figure 1: Searching AWS Marketplace for the Cartesia Sonic 3.6 SageMaker model package Figure 2: The Cartesia Sonic 3.6 listing in AWS Marketplace Figure 3: Creating a SageMaker model from the Sonic 3.6 subscription Figure 4: The SageMaker endpoint for Sonic 3.6 The model-package ARN is Region-specific. To verify the Sonic 3.6 package in US East (N. Virginia) with the SageMaker API, run: After the endpoint reaches InService , invoke it with the SageMaker Runtime InvokeEndpointWithResponseStream API and process the returned audio stream in your application. Some teams have existing GPU infrastructure, strict networking requirements, or a need to co-locate Cartesia with other services. For these cases, you can run the model container yourself on Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) GPU instances. This gives you full control over the runtime, scaling, and network path. It uses Cartesia’s container image, obtained from Cartesia, rather than the AWS Marketplace model package. Figure 5: Self-managed deployment flow for Cartesia Sonic on Amazon EC2 GPU instances Obtain the container image. Request the Sonic container image and licensing terms from Cartesia. Replicate it into your own private Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) repository so your compute plane can pull it with IAM-scoped credentials rather than reaching out to an external registry at scale. Choose your GPU instance family. Sonic runs on NVIDIA GPU instances. The G6 (L4) and G6e (L40S) families are the optimal balance for real-time TTS. The earlier G5 (A10G) also works. Match GPU memory and vCPU to your target concurrency and prefer a single-GPU instance per model replica for simplest scaling. Provision the compute plane (Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) or Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS)). For ECS: register a GPU task definition (set the container’s GPU resource requirement, for example, resourceRequirements with type GPU) and run it as a service behind an Application Load Balancer. For EKS: create a GPU node group (or Karpenter provisioner) using the EKS GPU-optimized AMI, install the NVIDIA device plugin, and deploy the container as a Deployment fronted by a Service/Ingress. Configure networking for low latency. Place inference nodes in a cluster placement group to minimize inter-node latency, keep replicas in a single Availability Zone for the tightest path, and use VPC endpoints for ECR/S3 pulls. For hybrid or on-premises callers, terminate traffic over AWS Direct Connect or a private Network Load Balancer to avoid public-internet hops. Load model weights efficiently.

item.title: StateBench: Testing how language models track state changes over long documents
item.abstract: Back to Articles StateBench: Testing how language models track state changes over long documents Enterprise Article Published November 3, 2026 Upvote 5 Kyle Wiggers Ai2Comms Follow allenai 📄 Tech Report | 🤗 Data | 💻 Code We’re introducing StateBench , a benchmark for long-context state tracking —how well language models keep track of information about entities in long documents as they evolve. State tracking underlies tasks from reading code, where variables are assigned and reassigned, to following a story as characters physically move around and objects change hands. For example, if a mystery novel states that “John gave Mary the knife” right before a murder occurs, it’s important to know that the state of each character has changed. However, not all state-tracking problems are created equal: some require only finding the latest update; harder ones require following a chain of changes, where one missed step can throw off the final answer. For example, a harder variant of our mystery state tracking would be if John gave Mary the item in his backpack, with it previously known that Edward put a knife in John’s backpack. Transformers have well-documented theoretical limits on hard variants of state tracking with long dependency chains, helping motivate recurrent and hybrid architectures such as Gated DeltaNet that carry a running memory forward. Existing state-tracking tests tend to focus on the hardest cases, but as these designs become more common, researchers need to know which kinds of state tracking each architecture can handle. We would like to understand the differences between architectures not just on the hardest kinds of state tracking, but also on the simpler, potentially more common kinds. To this end, we developed the StateBench benchmark to capture state-tracking problems of different complexity, which we used to evaluate the differences between language models with different architectures. We find that recurrent and hybrid models can generalize much farther than transformers when trained directly on these tasks, while frontier models including Gemini 3.8 Flash, Claude Opus 5.5, and GPT-6 Sol and Luna still break down on harder forms of state tracking as inputs grow longer. Four levels of state tracking StateBench consists of four difficulty levels that permit increasingly complex state update operations. For programmers, these levels of state tracking complexity can be understood as allowing different types of variable assignment operations: R-trivial problems use immutable assignment. A variable’s value never changes, so the model only needs to recover what it was first set to. In code, this looks like let x = 4; in everyday life, it’s like a birth date—it stays fixed. Aperiodic problems allow reassignment by value. The model needs to find the most recent value and can ignore earlier ones. In code, this looks like x = 4 followed later by x = 2; in everyday life, it’s like a thermostat, where the latest setting determines the current temperature. Soluble problems add self-referential updates. Each update builds on the current value, so the model has to carry changes forward rather than simply find the latest assignment. In code, this looks like x = x + 5; in everyday life, it’s like a game score, where each point adds to the running total. General finite problems add assignment by reference. One variable can take on another variable’s current value, creating dependencies across updates. In code, this looks like x = y or swapping two variables. Imagine a magician hiding a ball under one of five cups, then repeatedly swapping their positions. Finding the ball means keeping track of how those swaps change its location. This illustrates the S₅ state-tracking problem: following how successive swaps rearrange five objects. It belongs to the hardest of our four levels and is discussed in previous work on the limits of state tracking . These levels can be intuitively understood in terms of variable assignments, but they also represent theoretically motivated distinctions in state tracking rooted in Krohn–Rhodes theory, a branch of algebra that describes how state-tracking problems – which can be viewed as word problems over finite monoids – can be decomposed into atomic primitives. Each level in our hierarchy corresponds to a class of state-tracking problems that can be built out of a different set of primitives. To compare the four levels fairly, we start with a general finite sequence of variable assignments and derive three easier versions from it, producing four comparable StateBench problems—one at each difficulty level. All four use the same number of variables and distinct values, with assignments appearing at the same points in the sequence; only the type of assignment changes. What we found Pretrained models We tested a range of open pretrained models on the r-trivial, aperiodic, and general finite levels of StateBench to see where their state tracking breaks down, and whether different architectures fail where theory predicts. Under standard theoretical assumptions, transformers can handle r-trivial robustly (and soluble and aperiodic to some degree) but are predicted to fail on general problems. In contrast, Gated DeltaNet with a more flexible memory update can, in principle, handle all four levels. We started with open pretrained models, where the training data and context lengths are fully documented. These included two 7-billion-parameter models, Olmo 3 (a transformer) and Olmo Hybrid (which adds Gated DeltaNet layers), along with smaller models with 275 million and 2.7 billion parameters. All of these models were pretrained on the same data; none had seen contexts longer than 64,000 tokens during training, and we tested most of them on inputs well beyond that length. When we scored each model, almost all performed well on r-trivial problems, lost accuracy on aperiodic ones as inputs grew, and stayed at chance on general finite problems. Problem format mattered here—the 275-million-parameter hybrid and Gated DeltaNet models scored near the ceiling on RULER-style r-trivial problems but were near chance on the same problems framed as spreadsheet edits. That gap is one reason StateBench tests the same underlying problem in several formats. Frontier models We then tested four frontier models – Gemini 3.8 Flash, Claude Opus 5.5, and GPT-6 Sol and Luna – asking them to read each sequence of variable assignments and generate the final value of every variable. All four performed well on r-trivial and aperiodic problems. But on soluble and general finite problems, accuracy fell sharply as inputs grew longer, dropping to 13% or lower on the longest general finite problems. One likely factor is sensitivity ; at these harder levels, many more steps can affect the final answer, leaving less room for a model to miss an update without getting the result wrong. Models trained directly on the task Next, we investigated whether models’ difficulty with the harder levels reflects limits of the architectures themselves, or whether pretraining simply doesn’t teach models to solve them. Targeted direct training is a more favorable setting that reveals to what degree state-tracking issues come from the underlying architecture and optimizer rather than the data used to pretrain a model. We trained several 275-million-parameter models from scratch on StateBench: two transformer variants, two hybrids, and two Gated DeltaNet variants with different memory-update constraints. The models trained on sequences of up to 256 assignments and were tested on sequences as long as 64,000 assignments, or 250 times the maximum training length. The architectures began to diverge as sequences grew longer. Gated DeltaNet and hybrid models generalized almost perfectly on r-trivial, aperiodic, and soluble problems out to the longest sequences we tested, tens of thousands of assignments.

item.title: [AINews] LLMs can read & write neural network weights: "Weight Space Programming" cuts Autoresearch out of the RSI loop
item.abstract: Amid a deepening bear market for AI/tech (worthy of dark humor ) with Anthropic bonds receiving a “junk” rating and OpenAI fundraise headlines , we continue to see very surprising capability finds in the community, such as today. The best way to put today’s blockbuster paper in context is to recall Karpathy’s autoresearch from a mere 8 months ago , which presaged a summer of recursive self improvement fears : Abstractly, the demonstration is that you can take a sufficiently smart model and through running a series of experiments across a compute cluster, train a model autonomously without human expertise or intervention. However, this is usually done by an involved process of writing PyTorch/Jax code and running compute and watching loss curves and reading evals and optimizing kernels and data and…. Well, last month’s guest Alex Zhang comes back to coauthor a MONSTER discovery: what if you just ask a smart model to directly read and edit the weights of a dumber model? In ML this is the equivalent of not looking at source code, just directly seeing the 1’s and 0’s of ( very small ) compiled executables, and being able to 1) tell what they do , 2) oneshot-fix bugs given failed traces or, with 50 steps, improve in a general direction ( possible overstatement here ), 3) writing entire network weights from scratch in one shot , beating some independently trained models. If you believe that LLMs can truly fit and simulate everything given enough parameters (and in fact, LLMs are increasingly better calculators as you grow in size), then something like this was in theory bound to happen, but it is surprising nevertheless to have the ability suddenly emerge, as an independent reproduction seems to already have found: Of course the exact thing we are really modeling is some variant of mechanistic interpretability (which could be done by hand ), and right now unlikely to scale to more advanced tasks than simple games and RL policies, but the world has now gone from 0 to 1 on this very new RSI capability…. which will immediately put to use and explored due to its remarkable efficiency. AI News for 10/31/2026-11/02/2026. We checked 12 subreddits, 544 Twitters and no further Discords. AINews' website lets you search all past issues. As a reminder, AINews is now a section of Latent Space . You can opt in/out of email frequencies! DeepSeek Open-Sources a "Super-agent" Harness Prototype Release : DeepSeek Harness published a long design article ( article ) and the dsh-superagent-prototype repo ( repo link ). An official English version followed ( @tianyi ). Architecture : One long-lived router session talks to humans and hands out work. Isolated workers run tasks in parallel, triggered by GitHub events ( summary ). Claimed results : In DeepSeek's own test, p95 completion time fell from 29.5 to 15.7 min versus a single session using subagents ( summary ). Design rationale from a reviewer : Final reviewer 崔添翼 (@tianyi) says "Super" means a layer above the working agent, not superior intelligence. He frames the core trade-off as cross-task continuity versus throughput ( Zhihu summary ). Stated limits : The harness has no built-in cross-session long-term memory yet. Separating state, compute and environment is mostly unimplemented. The prototype has only been validated in a small, trusted internal environment, and security, privacy and agent-to-agent communication remain open questions. Prior art : He acknowledges that other teams explored similar architectures months earlier. Practitioner reception : @badlogicgames says the design matches where Earendil is heading: a single long-lived entity, ad-hoc recursive delegation and cross-system event triggers. @omarsar0 calls it a "masterclass" in coordination-execution harness design. DeepSeek also says it aims to support pi and other major harnesses with each model generation ( @tianyi ). Critique : @teortaxesTex calls the write-up "something of a hot mess." He argues DeepSeek builds internal crutches around model weaknesses such as hallucination rather than making the system generally robust. He also notes Bloomberg covered a repo that had no English announcement ( post ). V4.1 naming confusion : A Renmin University FlashRSI README referenced deepseek-v4.1-pro , which prompted release speculation. Teortaxes says it is a placeholder: the real config uses v4-flash and v4-pro, and deepseek-v4.1-flash is not a valid ID ( thread , follow-up ). He also says the API fingerprints for V4.1F-1017 are unchanged ( fingerprints ). Independent Evals and Frontier Model Signals GDPx benchmark (SemiAnalysis) : The benchmark covers 206 agentic tasks across 11 economically valuable domains, including chip design, SWE, finance and biology. The best model scores only 12% ( launch ). Results : Opus 5.5 leads at 12%. Gemini 4 Carbon is close behind at 10.9% at roughly 4x lower cost ( breakdown ). Reactions : @dylan522p apologized to Google, calling Carbon "spikier" but very strong in some areas. @demishassabis welcomed the benchmark. Analysis : @eliebakouch finds that removing safeguard-affected benchmarks changes the picture. In that view Carbon stays cheap, and Sol 6.1 is cheaper still. He also suggests OpenAI has stronger bio safeguards than Anthropic ( note ). Within-family comparison : Sol 6.1 and Astra score very similarly, Carbon beats Argon across the board, and Sonnet is strong at SWE ( comparison ). Possible bug : Some Argon cybersecurity runs may be affected by an Antigravity bug ( report ). Audit concerns : One satirical post complains that GDPx is not open source and is costly to audit ( post ). Epoch Capabilities Index : DeepSeek V4.1F-1017 scores 159, equal to GPT 5.5. That is 3 points above V4.1F-0910 and 10 above V4-Pro; Astra sits roughly 10 points higher ( @teortaxesTex ). Gap to Mythos : @scaling01 notes that no Chinese model has matched Mythos Preview (~161 ECI) after about 7 months. Weighting critique : @wenhaocha1 argues the unweighted ECI exaggerates the gap; weighting coding more heavily shrinks it to about 2 months. Spikiness : Teortaxes calls 1017 extremely spiky. It scores near zero on some SWE evals and approaches the frontier only on cybersecurity and quant trading ( chart ). He also flags "reward-hacking-shaped" behavior ( post ). October release roundup (Vals) : Vals reports 15 releases and more than 500B eval tokens ( @nikilravi ). Open-weight leaders : Kimi K3.1 Pro is #1 among open-weight models, with DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 close behind and stronger at cyber. New open models : Meta's Muse Spark Open (816B total, 42B active) is the most capable US open-weight model. Reflection's Beam 1.0 has 500B total parameters, 23B active and 1M context. Mistral's Le Chonk (1T total, 52B active) ranks #5 among open-weight models. Upcoming model rumors (unconfirmed) : GPT-6.2 Astra : Reportedly visible in Codex usage analytics, with a release "very soon" ( @kimmonismus , @TokenGremlin ). Mythos 5.5 : Appears in the HTML of Anthropic's site, which describes Mythos as "our most capable model class for cybersecurity and biology research" ( tip , text ). The tagline covers all Mythos models ( correction ). The mention is absent from an Oct 23 snapshot ( @AiBattle_ ). "Numbat" leak : The alleged Anthropic leak is likely fake, because parts of the weights exactly match random initialization ( @kimmonismus ). Research: Representations, Domain Data and Agent Collectives JEPA and the Platonic Representation Hypothesis : Balestriero and LeCun show that, under certain conditions, separately trained image and text JEPAs converge to essentially the same representation without paired data ( summary ). Claimed results : Their approach matches image-text alignment with 42x fewer samples than next-token prediction (21.6M vs 900M examples). A 109M text JEPA beats LLMs up to 72B on cross-modal alignment ( explainer ). Mechanism : The claimed driver is "two views of the same thing" training signals rather than scale.

item.title: Transformers Model Integration Contracts
item.abstract:
Back to Articles Transformers Model Integration Contracts Published November 3, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 12 +6 Tarek Ziadé tarekziade Follow On July 30, 2026, Transformers enabled PyTorch's scaled dot-product attention
(SDPA) for T5. As a side effect, UMT5's decoder could attend to future tokens.
During training, it could peek at the answer it was supposed to predict.
Nothing crashed, and the bug stayed in main for almost two months. When we later replayed those commits, a small UMT5 model running on CPU flagged
it on every one of them. This post is about that model and the tests built
around it. Why bugs reach main Transformers supports over 750
model types, and its test suite is big: 88,000+ CPU tests on main, plus
200,000+ GPU tests in a daily run. Model tests are only part of it: we also
test pipelines, training, distributed execution, quantization and attention
kernels. The integration tests load real checkpoints and exercise the model's API on
real hardware. Running all of that on every PR would mean keeping a lot of GPUs
busy all day long, which isn't practical. By the time a scheduled run finds a
regression, it may already be in main. Our approach is to shrink the model instead. We build a fixture : a small
model made from the real checkpoint's configuration, with fewer and narrower
layers but every kind of layer it has, and its tokenizer and processor files
unchanged. It is published once, then reused. We run "fast integration tests"
against it on a cheap CPU runner. In our CPU study ,
the experimental UMT5 fixture used 66 MB of weights; the source checkpoint
is 1,227 MB. This also covers very large models: some don't fit on our standard GPU
runners, but their fixtures run on CPU. Model integrators already build tiny test models (Transformers' tiny-random-* checkpoints). We wanted a common recipe, and
checks that go beyond loading the model and running a forward pass. The UMT5
bug would have passed a forward pass just fine. Fixtures won't replace full integration tests, but on PRs they give us a
chance to catch bugs before they reach main. Introducing Model Integration Contracts transformers-mic is a proposed
standard for packaging these tests. A Model Integration Contract (MIC) has
three parts: a fixture : the shrunk model described above, published once and pinned a usage path : a runnable Markdown example of something people do with the
model, such as generating text or running a training step baselines : the outputs recorded when running that example, reviewed by a
human The contract holds if running the usage path on the fixture still produces the
baselines. A contract covers an architecture and a usage path, not a single checkpoint:
compatible checkpoints can share a fixture, while each keeps its own expected
results. We publish them in huggingface-mic . For example, the SmolLM contract generates from prompts such as "The capital
of France is" and compares its token IDs with a recorded answer. After loading
the model and tokenizer, the generation code is, simplified to one prompt: inputs = tokenizer( "The capital of France is" , return_tensors= "pt" )
outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens= 4 , do_sample= False )
new_tokens = outputs[:, inputs[ "input_ids" ].shape[ 1 ]:] print (tokenizer.batch_decode(new_tokens, skip_special_tokens= True )) It also compares training loss, checks that gradients are finite and verifies
that an optimizer step changes the weights. See the full usage.md . A fleet dataset on the Hub pins each MIC to a frozen revision, along with the package versions
used to record its baselines. Each CI run records the fleet revision it
used, so we can reproduce it later. On a PR, we pick MICs based on the files the patch changes. The UMT5 regression We replayed frozen MICs over five months of Transformers commits. The small
UMT5 fixture flagged the regression from its introduction on July 30, 2026 until its fix on September 28 .
Label log-probabilities differed from the reviewed baseline by 1.22 and training
loss by about 0.20. One detail mattered: the contract used SDPA, the default attention path.
Running only the eager attention variant missed the bug. A fixture only
helps if it goes through the same code as the real checkpoint. We then reverted the fix on a proof branch in Transformers' CI. The check
failed with the same differences, and the selected T5 contract's runner step
took 13.4 seconds on CPU, excluding setup. The replay results and the CI demo have the measurements and reproduction details. How models are shrunk The first recipe was simple: make the dimensions smaller and keep fewer
layers. That wasn't enough for mixed architectures. Keeping two layers is no
use if both use sliding attention and the full-attention layers disappear. The recipe now has four steps: Shrink the configuration. Start from a real checkpoint and reduce
hidden sizes, attention heads and depth. Keep the different layer kinds,
including mixtures of sliding and full attention or dense and MoE layers.
Some architectures need extra rules to keep their components compatible.
We also look at the model's own Transformers tests: the ModelTester in test_modeling_<model>.py already picks a small config by hand, so we
take its sizes for any width our generic rule doesn't know by name. Keep preprocessing unchanged. Preserve vocabulary, special tokens and
input dimensions, and copy tokenizer and processor files byte for byte.
Loading and preprocessing are part of what we want to test. Build and validate the weights. Try seeded random weights and change
the inputs to check that the model responds. If it doesn't, try training
it on the contract's small batch of examples. Reload the saved model and
check that outputs, loss and gradients are finite. Reject failed builds. Freeze and record. Save the accepted weights and measure repeatable
outputs on a known-good Transformers build. Review the baselines for each
supported platform and precision, then publish a pinned snapshot. CI reuses
it; it does not rebuild the fixture for every PR. We also keep the original weights file format. Otherwise we would skip the
conversion code that runs when a user loads the real checkpoint. The full recipe has more detail. The Llama 4 Scout shrink report shows what this looks like on a big model. 108.6 billion parameters become 44.7
million. The vision stack goes from 34 layers to 2 and the language stack from
48 to 4, keeping the checked layer kinds and MoE routing style. Building MICs with agents Our CLI, tmic , creates the contract and builds the fixture. For a new
model, an LLM drafts the usage code and manifest, and CPU and GPU runs measure
the candidate baselines. The LLM drafts; it doesn't approve. Changed
expectations require human review. To try it on your machine, use your source checkpoint in place of org/model : pip install "transformers-mic[runtime]" "hf-doc-builder @ git+https://github.com/huggingface/doc-builder.git" hf auth login
tmic run org/model --local-only --fixtures-only --no-history --bill-to '' It drafts the contract, builds the fixture and records its baselines on your
machine, asking you to review each step, and stops before uploading anything.
For a new model, the draft comes from an LLM through Inference Providers, billed
to your own account ( --bill-to '' ). The CLI docs cover the individual steps. We used agents to build MICs across model families. When they hit an edge
case, we fixed the recipe itself rather than the one fixture, with help from
model experts. The published models and remaining gaps are in the coverage space . Random vs Overfit With random weights, our Whisper fixture barely responded to changes in
the audio. It ran, but that made it a poor test of the audio path. So we trained it on a few tones paired with words such as "red" and "green".
We weren't teaching it speech recognition, just making audio changes visible
in its outputs.

item.title: ServiceNow on-behalf-of token exchange with Bedrock AgentCore Gateway
item.abstract: AI agents that interact with enterprise APIs on behalf of users need to maintain user identity throughout the request chain. Without identity propagation, API calls arrive at downstream services as the application itself rather than the user who initiated the action. This breaks audit trails, bypasses user-level access controls, and violates the principle of least privilege. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. This post shows how to configure AgentCore Gateway , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, for an on-behalf-of (OBO) token exchange with Microsoft Entra ID. An AI agent can then call the ServiceNow REST API while preserving the calling user’s identity. You configure the token exchange on the gateway target, and AgentCore Gateway performs the exchange on each request. The pattern can be applied to other REST APIs protected by OAuth. In production, you can additionally pair identity propagation with Amazon Bedrock Guardrails to filter harmful content and validate the agent’s inputs and outputs. The architecture involves three key components connected through AgentCore Gateway: The following figure shows the end-to-end solution architecture, including components within AWS, Microsoft Entra ID, and ServiceNow. Figure 1: Solution architecture across AWS, Microsoft Entra ID, and ServiceNow As shown in Figure 1, the user acquires a JSON Web Token (JWT) to invoke the agent 1. The agent authenticates to the gateway with a JWT token scoped to the agent’s own application registration 2. The gateway then exchanges that token, using the OBO flow, for a new token scoped to the ServiceNow API connector, with the original user’s identity preserved 3. ServiceNow receives a valid token whose preferred_username claim maps to an existing ServiceNow user and applies that user’s permissions to the API call 4. When the agent calls the gateway, it presents a JWT with an audience claim matching the agent’s client ID (for example, 3ff88e17-XXXX-XXXX-XXXX-XXXXXXXXXXXX ). ServiceNow, however, expects a token with an audience claim matching its own API connector client ID ( 5d4a7a11-XXXX-XXXX-XXXX-XXXXXXXXXXXX ). The OBO flow bridges this gap. AgentCore Gateway sends the inbound token to the Entra token endpoint along with the agent application’s client credentials, the target scope, and a parameter requested_token_use: on_behalf_of . Entra validates that the calling user consented to the delegation, then issues a new token for the ServiceNow API with the original user’s claims intact. Before you begin, you need the following: Start by creating an application registration to represent the ServiceNow API connector. The following screenshot shows the application registration page for the ServiceNow API Connector in Microsoft Entra ID. Figure 2: Application registration for the ServiceNow API connector in Microsoft Entra ID After creating, in the Overview page note the Application (client) ID. In the navigation menu expand Manage and select Expose an API and add a scope named user_impersonation using the default Application ID URI. This scope is what the OBO flow requests when exchanging tokens. The following screenshot shows how to expose an API in Microsoft Entra ID. Figure 3: Exposing the user_impersonation scope in Microsoft Entra ID Next, create an application registration for the AI agent. The following screenshot shows the application registration page in Microsoft Entra ID for the ServiceNow Agent application. Figure 4: Application registration for the ServiceNow Agent in Microsoft Entra ID Note the Application (client) ID for the ServiceNowAgent. Create a client secret on this registration. The gateway needs these credentials to perform the OBO exchange. The following screenshot shows how you can create a client secret on the ServiceNow Agent application registration in Microsoft Entra ID. Figure 5: Creating a client secret on the ServiceNow Agent application registration Then configure the agent application to have API permissions to call the ServiceNow API connector application. The following screenshot shows the API permissions that you need to configure on the ServiceNow Agent application registration in Microsoft Entra ID. Figure 6: API permission configuration in Microsoft Entra ID No changes to the Entra configuration are needed beyond what you would set up for any standard OBO integration between two applications. In the ServiceNow administrative console, navigate to System OAuth > Inbound Integrations and create a new inbound integration (Third party ID token issued by OIDC supporting identity provider). Specify the client ID from the ServiceNow API connector application registration you created in Entra. The following screenshot shows the configuration of the inbound integration in ServiceNow. Figure 7: Configuring the inbound integration in ServiceNow In the same screen, create a new OpenID Connect (OIDC) provider configuration and enter the OIDC metadata URL for your Entra tenant. Map the user claim to the appropriate user field. For example, if your Entra tenant places the user’s email in the preferred_username claim, map that to the Email field in ServiceNow. Clear JTI verification if your Entra tenant doesn’t include it in tokens. Entra uses an internal claim named uti on tokens it issues, which is equivalent to JTI. Consider mapping this uti claim to a jti claim to provide additional replay protection and denylisting. The following screenshot shows how to configure the OIDC provider in ServiceNow. Figure 8: Configuring the OAuth OIDC provider in ServiceNow Finally, in the same screen, create an auth scope for the integration (for example, APIConnector ). The following screenshot shows how to create a new auth scope in ServiceNow. Figure 9: Creating a new auth scope in ServiceNow Limit the auth scope to the Table API, or whichever ServiceNow APIs your agent needs to access, as shown in the following screenshot. Figure 10: Limiting the auth scope to the Table API in ServiceNow After this configuration is complete, ServiceNow accepts authorization tokens with an audience of your API connector’s client ID and resolves the calling user from the preferred_username claim. With Entra and ServiceNow configured, you can now set up AgentCore Gateway to handle the OBO exchange natively. Create a new outbound auth configuration (choose Build > Identity > Add Outbound Auth > Add OAuth client ) in AgentCore and select Customized provider . Enter the client ID and client secret from your agent application registration, along with the Entra discovery URL as shown in the following screenshot. Figure 11: Adding an OAuth client in AgentCore Gateway Expand Additional configurations and select JWT authorization grant as shown in the following screenshot. This tells the gateway to use a JWT-based grant type for token exchange. Figure 12: Configuring the JWT authorization grant Create a new AgentCore Gateway ( Build > Gateways > Create gateway ). When defining the gateway details, expand Additional configurations — optional and select MCP version 2025-11-25 as shown in the following screenshot. This version is required for native OBO support. You can’t turn on native OBO for gateways created with earlier MCP versions. Figure 13: Selecting MCP version 2025-11-25 Configure the inbound identity using your agent’s application registration (select Use existing identity provider configurations ), as you would for any gateway that accepts Entra-authenticated requests. Under JWT Authorization Configuration add the Application ID we documented earlier for the ServiceNowAgent as shown in the following screenshot. Figure 14: Configuring inbound authorization in AgentCore Gateway Add a target to the gateway pointing to your ServiceNow REST endpoint. Define the schema inline.

item.title: Claude Platform now supports native OpenTelemetry observability in Databricks MLflow
item.abstract: An agent can return a plausible answer while missing an important finding or reading the same source repeatedly. The answer alone won't explain why. Traces show the model and tool calls behind it, so you can investigate the failure, find related cases, and test whether a change helps. Databricks MLflow is now a supported destination for native OpenTelemetry export from the Claude Platform.. With native export to Databricks MLflow, developers using the Anthropic SDKs, the Messages API and Managed Agents can send native traces to Databricks and use MLflow to debug their agents and evaluate changes. MLflow Tracing is built on OpenTelemetry, an open standard for collecting and exporting service signals. A trace records an agent’s execution as individual steps, called spans, such as model requests and tool calls. Claude’s native instrumentation generates these spans and exports them using the OpenTelemetry Protocol. Databricks receives the spans through Zerobus Ingest and stores them in Unity Catalog tables linked to an MLflow experiment. You can inspect Claude traces alongside traces from other instrumented services, with the same tools for debugging and evaluation. Unity Catalog controls access to the data, which you can also query with SQL. With the combination of Zerobus and Unity Catalog, enterprises can get two crucial benefits: low-latency trace ingestion at high QPS plus the ability to govern access to the sensitive data stored in agentic traces. In Databricks, open the Experiments tab and click Create Experiment . Under Trace storage location , keep Unity Catalog selected. Choose an existing catalog and schema. This creates new MLflow experiments linked to the Unity Catalog table that stores OpenTelemetry traces. The detailed setup guide covers permissions and SQL warehouse requirements. Set the Databricks destination using your workspace ID, region, and spans table. The Zerobus connection guide explains how to obtain a table-scoped OAuth token. The new native OTel integrations cover Anthropic SDKs, the Messages API, and Managed Agents. For the Anthropic SDK, install the packages below and configure an OTel tracer provider and exporter to create spans for Anthropic SDK calls. Follow Claude Platform OpenTelemetry guide to send traces from the Messages API and Claude Managed Agent your Databricks destination. Claude Code and Claude Agent SDK also support OpenTelemetry. To send their traces to the same destination, set these additional variables before starting your application: Run your Claude agent, then open Traces in the experiment. Open a trace to inspect its model calls, tool activity, timing, and captured inputs and outputs. Note that inputs and outputs are captured only if you opt in by setting content mode to “full”. Once Claude traces arrive in MLflow, you can use them throughout development. A trace provides a record for debugging, a case for expert review, and evidence for evaluating the next version of an agent. An unexpected answer can come from missing context, a failed tool call, or how the model used a tool result. MLflow’s Analyze trace action brings Genie Code into the investigation. It examines the recorded execution and helps explain where things went wrong. Ask follow-up questions about missing context, failed tool calls, or expensive steps, to inspect the relevant context behind the explanation. This helps you decide whether to revise instructions, improve a tool, or change the context available to the agent. MLflow Issues , available in Beta, uses Genie Code to identify recurring quality and operational problems. It examines responses, tool calls, timing, errors, and assessments, then groups related findings with links to the supporting traces. Examples include repeated searches that waste tokens, missing arguments that cause tool failures, and responses that don’t follow the required format. You can schedule detection to keep this analysis running as new traces arrive. Teams can choose how often it runs, use metadata or tags to focus on particular traffic, and customize the types of problems it looks for. After a fix, an issue monitor can track whether the problem returns. MLflow creates a scorer for the issue, evaluates recent traces to establish a baseline, and scores a sample of new traces to measure its frequency over time. Some quality judgments require domain knowledge. MLflow Review Queues bring that expertise into the development process through selected traces and questions tailored to the agent. Reviewers can assess the recorded request and response, explain what is missing, and provide an expected answer. Their feedback helps developers refine the agent and establish reference answers for subsequent evaluations. A change to instructions, tools, or skills can fix one failure while introducing another. Traces also make agent behavior measurable. Run MLflow Agent Evaluation on Claude traces to test whether a change to prompts, skills, tools, improve the agent or regress. For example, the following code executes an LLM judge to examine whether an agent makes redundant tool calls. When the original and revised agents have run against the same cases, their evaluation runs can be compared using the same judges. Click Compare in MLflow UI to see scores and responses side by side, with the underlying traces available to explain remaining failures. The same approach works for checks such as whether an agent followed a required workflow or used the appropriate tools. Testing and Refining Claude Code Skills with MLflow demonstrates how these checks and their rationales can guide improvements to skills.
